extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning discrete mathematics and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, examples, and basic theorems about relations (relations as subsets of Cartesian products, domain/range, inverse, composition) aimed at teaching proof techniques and intuition (pictures, examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A and B are sets. Then a set R ⊆ A × B is called a relation from A to B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: think of truth sets of statements P(x,y) as relations; but any subset of A×B qualifies. Examples given (finite sets, greater-than on R, membership relation to power set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain of a relation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: set of all first coordinates of ordered pairs in R. Example: domain of the 'student lives in room' relation is all students who live in some dorm room. Use existential introduction in proofs about domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of a relation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: set of all second coordinates occurring in R. Example: range of the 'student lives in room' relation is the set of occupied dorm rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inverse contains the same ordered pairs with coordinates reversed. Examples: inverse of greater-than is less-than; inverse of 'student enrolled in course' swaps course and student. Note domain/range swap: Dom(R^{-1}) = Ran(R), Ran(R^{-1}) = Dom(R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If R ⊆ A × B and S ⊆ B × C then S ◦ R = {(a,c) ∈ A × C | ∃b ∈ B((a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that the second coordinates in R and first coordinates in S come from the same set B. Notational warning: if (s,c) ∈ E and (c,p) ∈ T then (s,p) ∈ T ◦ E (order reverses the appearence). Examples: students→courses→professors producing a student→professor relation. Composition is generally non-commutative but associative (T◦(S◦R) = (T◦S)◦R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infix notation for relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a relation from A to B, x ∈ A, and y ∈ B, sometimes write x R y to mean (x,y) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful shorthand when reasoning about relational statements (e.g., s E c means student s is enrolled in course c). Composition can be described as: S ◦ R = {(a,c) | ∃b(a R b and b S c)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial representation / directed graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations can be drawn as arrows from elements of A to elements of B (or as directed graphs for relations on A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain = vertices in A with arrows leaving them; range = vertices in B with arrows entering them. Loops represent (x,x) ∈ R. Pictures help visualize composition (two-step paths correspond to composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity relation
rubrics_metrics.description: i_A = {(x,x) | x ∈ A}, the identity relation on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i_A is a relation on A; it satisfies ∀x(x = x). Useful in properties: R ◦ i_A = R and i_B ◦ R = R for relations R ⊆ A×B. Also used in characterizing reflexivity (i_A ⊆ R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is reflexive on A if ∀x ∈ A((x,x) ∈ R) (i.e., ∀x ∈ A(x R x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphically: loops at every vertex. Example: Dr (|x−x|<r) is reflexive. Characterization: R is reflexive iff i_A ⊆ R (Theorem 4.3.4 part 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is symmetric if ∀x ∈ A∀y ∈ A(x R y → y R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphically: whenever there is an edge from x to y there is one from y to x (non-loop edges come in opposite pairs). Characterization: R is symmetric iff R = R^{-1} (Theorem 4.3.4 part 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is transitive if ∀x ∈ A∀y ∈ A∀z ∈ A((x R y ∧ y R z) → x R z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition view: R is transitive iff R ◦ R ⊆ R (Theorem 4.3.4 part 3). Example: greater-than is transitive; Dr (|x−y|<r) need not be transitive (counterexample provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: (R^{-1})^{-1} = R
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverse of the inverse of R equals R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: show biconditional membership for an arbitrary ordered pair (a,b) ∈ A×B by unfolding definitions: (a,b) ∈ (R^{-1})^{-1} iff (b,a) ∈ R^{-1} iff (a,b) ∈ R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain/Range swap for inverse
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show element-wise equivalences using existential quantifiers and the definition of inverse. Both sides are subsets of the appropriate ambient set (B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Associativity of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If R: A→B, S: B→C, T: C→D then T ◦ (S ◦ R) = (T ◦ S) ◦ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by taking an arbitrary (a,d) and showing membership in each side via existential witnesses: introduce c from the outer composition and b from the inner composition. The text demonstrates one direction and leaves the other as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: (S ◦ R)^{-1} = R^{-1} ◦ S^{-1}
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverse of a composition reverses the order: (S ◦ R)^{-1} = R^{-1} ◦ S^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute both sides using definitions and existential quantifiers; examples with E (enrollment) and T (teaching) illustrate the equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain of a composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Dom(S ◦ R) ⊆ Dom(R). If Ran(R) ⊆ Dom(S) then Dom(S ◦ R) = Dom(R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof ideas: membership in Dom(S ◦ R) asserts existence of b such that (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S, which implies (a,b) ∈ R so a ∈ Dom(R). The equality condition requires Ran(R) ⊆ Dom(S) to ensure every a ∈ Dom(R) can be extended to a c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antisymmetric (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is antisymmetric if ∀x ∈ A∀y ∈ A((x R y ∧ y R x) → x = y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ≤ on R and ⊆ on sets are antisymmetric. Antisymmetry captures the idea that mutual relatedness forces equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial and total orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial order is a relation on A that is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric. A total order is a partial order satisfying ∀x∀y(x R y ∨ y R x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: partial orders express a notion of 'at least as large as' without requiring comparability of every pair; total orders require comparability. Examples: ≤ and ⊆ are partial orders; adding totality yields a total order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy: handling ordered pairs and existentials
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements about relations use ordered pairs as the universe for elements of relations and introduce existential witness variables for composition/other existential statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: to prove (R^{-1})^{-1}=R introduce arbitrary (a,b) ∈ A×B; to prove associativity introduce c from C and then b from B. The commentary emphasizes choosing appropriate variables and proving biconditionals by element-chasing.
